headline: Meet the Tilcayo: A Cat Species Hidden for 1.4 Million Years
meta_description: Scientists confirm the tilcayo is a new feline species in Bolivia's Yungas cloud forest—the first documented cat species in over 100 years.
summary_short: DNA analysis reveals the tilcayo of Bolivia is a distinct species that local communities knew all along. It's the first new living feline named in over a century.
body:
For over a century, science missed what Bolivia's local communities already knew: the tilcayo is its own species. A genetic study published in Current Biology has now formally confirmed what indigenous people called this small spotted cat—Leopardus tilcayo—is not a Brazilian tiger cat variant, but a genetically distinct lineage that diverged 1.4 million years ago. The discovery marks the first new living feline species to be formally named in more than 100 years, and it emerged not from a dramatic jungle expedition, but from scientists finally having the DNA tools to see what their eyes could not.

The tilcayo weighs only about 3 pounds and measures roughly 18 inches long—smaller than most house cats. Its light brown fur bears irregularly shaped rosettes, and camera traps reveal it hunts at night, feeding primarily on rodents. Yet almost nothing else is documented. Only two live individuals have been directly examined by researchers, including a 10-year-old male now at the Senda Verde wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia, where he lives after years as a household pet.

The real story lies in what this discovery exposes about the gaps in our knowledge. When researchers analyzed DNA from 38 cats across South America, including museum specimens, they found that tiger cats are not two species as previously thought, but five genetically distinct lineages. What changed was not the cat—it has lived in Bolivia's Yungas cloud forest for over a million years—but our ability to see it clearly. Local communities were simply ahead of the science.

Yet naming the tilcayo feels bittersweet. Its only confirmed habitat faces relentless pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, fires, and mining. The research team believes it could qualify as endangered rather than merely vulnerable. As one senior researcher noted, the discovery carries a sobering message: many undiscovered species exist in places that may not survive long enough to be studied.
quick_facts: Tilcayo weighs about 3 pounds, smaller than most house cats
First new living feline species named in over 100 years
DNA analysis shows it split from other tiger cats 1.4 million years ago
Only found in Bolivia's Yungas cloud forest, facing deforestation
Local Bolivian communities named it tilcayo long before science confirmed it
